Neonates of Liolaemus wiegmannii emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of 2.2 cm [Lb = 2.2 cm], a modest size that underscores the altricial nature of this saxicolous lizard. This measurement was obtained from a cohort of captive-born individuals whose mothers were collected from the coastal dune systems of Argentina. Hatchlings are immediately capable of exogenous feeding, typically consuming small arthropods within the first day of emergence. The incubation period, during which the embryo is nurtured within the cleidoic egg, is highly dependent on thermal conditions. When eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the interval from oviposition to eclosion is 56 days [ab = 56 days], a duration that reflects the relatively low metabolic rates characteristic of this cool-temperate lineage. This extended incubation period aligns well with values reported for other members of the Liolaemus boulengeri group, which also experience protracted embryonic development under similar thermal regimes. The synchronous hatching observed in most clutches suggests a degree of embryonic metabolic coordination, likely an adaptation to the unpredictable thermal environment of their native Patagonian sand dunes.

As juveniles grow, their progression through life stages is marked by the attainment of specific body size thresholds rather than chronological age alone, a pattern common among lizards with indeterminate growth. Upon reaching a snout-vent length of 4.2 cm [Lp = 4.2 cm], individuals typically undergo gonadal activation and become capable of reproduction. This onset of puberty is a critical life-history transition, as it represents the shift from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes investment in reproductive effort. Data from mark-recapture studies conducted over several field seasons indicate that the ultimate snout-vent length achieved by adults in this species is 5.8 cm [Li = 5.8 cm], a value that appears to be genetically constrained. Females at this ultimate size are capable of carrying the largest clutches, though body condition and resource availability play a more prominent role in determining annual fecundity than does absolute body size alone. The relatively modest size at both puberty and adulthood suggests that this species prioritizes early reproduction over continued somatic expansion, a strategy often observed in short-lived lizards occupying seasonally variable habitats.

The maximum adult body mass observed in Liolaemus wiegmannii is 3.84 grams [Wwi = 3.84 grams], a figure derived from gravid females measured during the austral spring. This value was calculated by scaling from the known mass-length relationship of the closely related wall lizard Podarcis muralis, adjusting for the differences in asymptotic body length between the two species. This mass is quite modest even by liolaemid standards, reflecting the species' relatively small body size and its occupation of a high-energy, low-stability environment where maintaining a large body would impose excessive metabolic costs. In practice, most adults sampled in the wild weigh between 3.0 and 3.8 grams, with individuals in prime condition occasionally exceeding the asymptotic estimate during periods of high prey abundance. This relatively low adult mass also has implications for the species' reproductive output, as female body volume directly limits the physical space available for developing eggs within the coelomic cavity.

Reproductive output in Liolaemus wiegmannii is characterized by moderate fecundity and multiple breeding events per season, a pattern common among small liolaemids occupying temperate habitats. Gravid females produce clutches ranging from 3 to 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 8 eggs per clutch], with clutch size correlating positively with maternal snout-vent length. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active season (20 °C [T = 20 °C]), females are capable of producing between three and four clutches per year [F_R_i = between three and four clutches per year], resulting in a substantial annual reproductive investment. This rate of reproduction is made possible by the species' ability to store sperm from a single insemination and the rapid vitellogenesis that follows each oviposition. The maximum annual egg production, calculated by multiplying the largest clutch size by the highest clutch frequency, yields a peak fecundity of approximately 32 eggs per female per year under ideal conditions. These findings position Liolaemus wiegmannii as an r-selected strategist relative to its larger, longer-lived congeners in the high Andes.

Longevity data for Liolaemus wiegmannii, based on field observations of marked individuals and extrapolated from the closely related species Liolaemus pictus, indicate a maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years] at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This lifespan is relatively short for a reptile of this body size, underscoring the high mortality rates associated with its exposed, low-latitude habitat. Predation by birds, snakes, and small mammals is intense, and few individuals survive beyond their third reproductive season in the wild. The age-structured demographic data suggest that this species exhibits a Type III survivorship curve, with extremely high mortality among hatchlings and juveniles, followed by a relatively stable adult mortality rate. The rapid progression to a snout-vent length of 4.2 cm [Lp = 4.2 cm] during the first year allows individuals to participate in at least one breeding season before the odds of mortality become overwhelming, and the combination of high annual fecundity and an 8-year maximum lifespan (8 years) [am = 8 years] collectively paints a picture of a life history finely tuned to exploit ephemeral resources in a disturbance-prone ecosystem at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
